ゆうひ の とりい — The gate at sunset (N5 review)
You link actions in time (～てから, ～た あと で, ～まえ に) and review all the N5 grammar in a story: the last day in Japan.
After eating, I go for a walk.
Before going to bed I brush my teeth.
This trip is a memory for life.
To link two actions in time: ～て から (after, straight after).
To use ～た あと で (after) and compare it with ～まえ に (before).
To review all the verb forms: ～ます, dictionary, ～て, ～ない, ～た.
To review the N5 particles: は, が, を, に, で, へ, と, から, まで, も, の.
To read the longest story so far, with almost no help.
The last day in Japan. In the morning, Mihai and Ana say goodbye to Haruka and Sakura. This evening they leave Hiroshima, but first they’re going to Miyajima once more.
Are you really going home today?
Yes. But we’re not leaving straight away. First we’re going to Miyajima, then to the airport.
Sakura, you have school today, don’t you? After school finishes, we’ll go to the station to see them off.
Haruka, thank you so much for everything.
No, thank you. Give our regards to Kenji. And…
(Whispering) Good luck. Today the tide starts going out at around four in the afternoon.
What are you two talking about?
Hee-hee-hee. Come on, have a good trip.
We’re off! Sakura, see you later!
“osewa ni narimashita” = thank you for everything you’ve done
“kochira koso” = it’s I who should thank you
Run it together, no pause: “tabete-kara”. Your voice doesn’t drop after て.
The most used phrases in any Japanese home: it-te ki-mas (the person leaving), it-te ras-shai (the person staying).
gan-bat-te: the っ pause before て. You say it to anyone facing something difficult.
The ～て form + から = “after…, (then)”. It shows that the second action comes STRAIGHT AFTER the first, usually as part of a plan:
After doing my homework, I watch television.
First we’re going to Miyajima, then to the airport.
Don’t confuse: ～て から = “after” (time). But a clause + から = “because” (chapter 8). たべて から = after eating. たべます から = because I eat.
2. ～た あと で and ～まえ に
X の あと で
A symmetrical trap: BEFORE uses the dictionary form (even in the past!). AFTER uses the ～た form (even in the future!). あした しごと が おわった あと で あいましょう (Tomorrow, after work finishes, let’s meet).
～て から and ～た あと で mean almost the same. ～て から stresses the order (“first X, then Y”). ～た あと で stresses the moment (“after X”).

ミハイ の にっき — Mihai’s diary, the last page
On the plane home, Mihai writes the last page of his travel diary, without looking in the dictionary.
Thirteen days have already passed since we came to Japan.
On the first day I got lost in Shinjuku, got a fright from nattō and so on.
Tokyo was big and lively. Kyoto was quiet and beautiful.
In Kyoto we met Mrs Suzuki’s sister. I think it’s wonderful that the two of them can talk again.
In Hiroshima, Kenji’s family was very kind to us.
Sakura cried at the station. She said many times: “Come again!”
And at Miyajima something happened that I will never forget as long as I live.
What exactly… you’ll probably understand if you look at the left hand of the person sleeping next to me.
I’m truly glad I learned Japanese.
“yō ni natte” = have become able to…
“yasashiku shite kuremashita” = were kind to us

ゆうひ の とりい — The gate at sunset
At three in the afternoon, the two of them arrived at Miyajima once more.
Today there were few people, and the island was quiet.
“You again? I haven’t got a map today!” Mihai laughed.
But Mihai’s hand stayed in his pocket the whole time. In his pocket was a little box.
That morning he had taken it from the bottom of his bag and put it in his pocket. He wasn’t going to make the same mistake twice.
It was four o’clock. Just as Haruka had said, the sea water was going further and further out.
Under the gate that had been standing in the sea until a little earlier, the sand began to appear.
“Look! We can walk to the gate!” Ana shouted.
They took off their shoes and walked across the cold sand.
Seen up close, the gate was truly enormous.
The red pillars were old and thick and smelled of the sea.
Lots of coins were tucked into the little cracks in the pillars.
“They say you make a wish and push in a coin,” said Ana.
Ana put in a five-yen coin and closed her eyes.
“What did you wish for?” “It’s a secret.”
The sun began to set. The sky, the sea and the sand all turned orange.
Mihai took a deep breath. Now was the moment.
“Yes?” Ana turned round. Her face was glowing in the light of the sunset.
Mihai took the little box out of his pocket and knelt on the sand.
Quietly, line by line, he said the words he had written in his notebook the night before.
“When we met, you were my Spanish teacher.”
“Then we learned Japanese together. In hard times and happy ones, you were always by my side.”
“When you laugh, my heart grows warm.”
Mihai opened the little box. The blue ring sparkled in the light of the sunset.
“I want to be with you for the rest of my life. Marry me.”
A tear fell from her eyes, then another.
“…It’s not fair to say it to me in Japanese.”
“Now I have to answer you in Japanese too.”
Ana wiped her tears and smiled. Then she said quietly but clearly:
With trembling hands, Mihai put the ring on the ring finger of her left hand.
The size was perfect. Exactly as Haruka had said.
The deer was watching them from a distance.
“That deer must have come to apologise for the map,” said Mihai.
That evening, at the station, Sakura noticed Ana’s ring.
Haruka didn’t say anything; she just gave Mihai a small nod.
The train set off. Sakura ran to the end of the platform and kept waving.
“Come again! And invite me to the wedding!”
For the fourteen hours of the flight, Ana kept looking at her ring.
On the last page of his diary, Mihai wrote: “I’m truly glad I learned Japanese.”
At Madrid airport, Yuki, Kenji and Mrs Suzuki were waiting for them.
They looked at each other and answered together: “We’re home!”
— The end of the N5 level. But their journey in Japanese has only just begun.

Next spring, it’s Mihai and Ana’s wedding.
